text.p: Australian scientists began on Monday to harvest a crop of genetically-engineered potatoes which do not turn brown after being cut or bruised.

Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) researcher Simon Robinson said the government agency had copied the gene, or DNA sequence, which makes potatoes turn brown if they are not quickly cooked.

"By putting the gene back-to-front, or a slightly altered version of the gene back into potato plants, it blocks the browning gene," said Robinson, adding that the technology should not affect any other characteristic of the fruit.
Robinson said the technology could be applied to apples, bananas, pears, lettuces and other fruit and vegetables and could achieve significant savings for processors and consumers.
"At the moment, with potatoes in Australia alone, there are probably A$5-10 million (US$4-8 million) worth of losses each year due to bruising," he said.

Following a small field trial last year, 1,000 plants (about one tonne of potatoes) were grown in the Adelaide hills in southern Australia to test the transgenic potatoes for yield, cooking quality and tuber size.

Robinson said similar work was being done in the United States and The Netherlands, but the CSIRO had patented the technology worldwide and he believed commercial production of the process was about five years away.
The CSIRO has signed a licensing agreement for apples and pears with Canadian group Okanagan Biotechnology Inc and is negotiating agreements for potatoes, bananas, and lettuces.
